items.note: Goes before the main verb (or after 'be'): 'She also speaks French.'
Followed by a noun or -ing: 'French as well as Spanish.'
Casual spoken/written: 'Plus, it's free.'
Adds an extra argument; also a preposition + -ing: 'Besides being cheap...'
Adds a stronger point: 'What's more, it's free.'
Piles on another point, often a negative.
'In addition, ...' or 'in addition to + noun'.
Starts a new sentence in formal writing; comma after.
Adds a stronger, supporting point in formal writing.
Joins two clauses: 'It was cheap, but it broke.'
Starts a new sentence; comma after: 'It was cheap. However, it broke.'
Introduces a clause: 'Although it was cold, we went out.'
Stronger than although; followed by a clause.
Compares two facts: 'He is shy, whereas she is outgoing.'
Contrasts two ideas when used mid-sentence.
Presents the opposite side of a topic.
Shows a clear difference between two things.
Means 'in spite of that'; starts a new clause.
Followed by a clause: 'because it was late.'
Followed by a noun: 'because of the rain.'
Gives a known reason at the start: 'Since it was late, we left.'
Gives a reason at the start of a sentence; also 'as' = while.
Followed by a noun phrase: 'due to bad weather.'
Formal alternative to 'due to'.
Positive cause: 'Thanks to your help...'
Followed by a noun: 'as a result of the merger.'
Formal and a bit old-fashioned; noun phrase.
Joins two clauses: 'It rained, so we stayed in.'
'That's why + clause' highlights the result.
Starts a new sentence; comma after.
Logical conclusion: 'We lost data; therefore, we must restart.'
Result of a previous event or action.
Very formal, often in academic writing.
Very formal; often followed by a noun phrase.
Refers back to a cause just mentioned.
Introduces a single example: 'For example, ...'
Same use as 'for example'.
Followed by a noun list in the middle of a sentence.
Informal for 'such as': 'sports like tennis.'
Followed by a noun: 'including HR and Finance.'
Highlights one important item: 'in particular...'
Emphasises one item among others.
Gives the exact thing you mean.
Begins a series of points.
Used with 'then', 'next' in instructions.
Next step in an informal sequence.
Follows 'first' in instructions.
Neutral transition to the next step.
Later; used without 'that'.
During the waiting period.
After a long time or effort.
Formal; 'later' in reports.
Followed by a noun or -ing: 'despite the rain.'
Same as despite, but with 'of'.
Concedes a point before disagreeing.
Adds a balanced or generous point.
Concessive adverb: 'It's old. Still, it works.'
Reminds the reader of a key reason.
Introduces your view.
Honest, direct opinion.
Final judgement after weighing everything.

items.s: I need to buy milk, and ____ some bread.
items.note: 'And also' adds one more item.

items.s: She speaks Spanish as well ____ French.
items.note: 'As well as' means 'and also'.

items.s: The plan is cost-effective. ____, it is environmentally friendly.
items.note: 'Furthermore' adds a supporting point in formal writing.

items.s: The report is late. On top of ____, it contains several errors.
items.note: 'On top of that' is a fixed phrase that piles on another problem.

items.s: The proposal lacks funding; ____, it ignores the legal constraints altogether.
items.note: 'Moreover' adds a stronger point; the other options express contrast or result.

items.s: I'm tired. ____, I have a headache.
items.note: 'Plus' is casual for 'and also'.

items.s: ____ being cheap, the hotel was spotless.
items.note: 'Besides' can precede an -ing form; 'moreover' and 'furthermore' can't.

items.s: Not only did she finish early, ____ she also saved money.
items.note: 'Not only... but also' is a correlative pair.

items.s: We would like to thank you for your support. ____, we would like to invite you to our launch event.
items.note: 'In addition' adds a new point in a polite email.

items.s: I wanted to go out, ____ it was raining.
items.note: 'But' joins two contrasting clauses.

items.s: ____ it was cold, we went swimming.
items.note: 'Although' is followed by a full clause.

items.s: ____ the cold, we went swimming.
items.note: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase or -ing.

items.s: The migration was expensive; ____, the board approved it.
items.note: 'Nevertheless' = in spite of that. Needs a clause after it.

items.s: Some employees prefer remote work, ____ others value the office.
items.note: 'Whereas' compares two facts in one sentence.

items.s: Remote work saves commuting time. ____, it can feel isolating.
items.note: 'On the other hand' starts a new sentence with a contrasting point.

items.s: The results were promising, ____ the sample size was small.
items.note: 'Even though' is followed by a clause. 'In spite' lacks 'of'.

items.s: I like the flat, ____ it's a bit small.
items.note: 'But' links a positive and a negative point casually.

items.s: Sales fell in Europe. ____, they rose sharply in Asia.
items.note: 'In contrast' marks a clear difference.

items.s: I stayed home ____ I was ill.
items.note: 'Because' gives the reason.

items.s: I stayed home ____ my illness.
items.note: 'Because of' + noun.

items.s: ____ it was late, we took a taxi.
items.note: 'Since' at the start gives a known reason.

items.s: The flight was cancelled ____ bad weather.
items.note: 'Due to' is followed by a noun phrase.

items.s: Services were interrupted ____ a power failure.
items.note: 'Owing to' + noun, formal. 'Because/since/as' need a clause.

items.s: ____ the new policy, productivity has improved.
items.note: 'Thanks to' gives a positive cause with a noun.

items.s: The outage occurred ____ a misconfigured firewall rule.
items.note: 'As a result of' + noun phrase; 'as a result' stands alone.

items.s: ____ the server crashed, we lost all unsaved data.
items.note: 'Because' takes a clause; 'because of' and 'due to' need a noun.

items.s: I couldn't call you ____ my phone died.
items.note: 'Because' + clause.

items.s: It was raining, ____ we stayed inside.
items.note: 'So' introduces the result.

items.s: He didn't study. ____, he failed the exam.
items.note: 'As a result' shows the consequence.

items.s: The system was overloaded; ____, response times increased.
items.note: 'Consequently' links a cause and its result.

items.s: Costs have risen sharply; ____, we must revise the budget.
items.note: 'Therefore' introduces a logical conclusion.

items.s: The data is incomplete, ____ no firm conclusion can be drawn.
items.note: 'Thus' introduces a result in formal writing.

items.s: I lost my keys, ____ I couldn't get in.
items.note: 'So' joins a cause and result informally.

items.s: She was late, and ____ she missed the start.
items.note: 'As a result' stands alone; 'as a result of' needs a noun.

items.s: The vendor went bankrupt. That's ____ we changed suppliers.
items.note: 'That's why' introduces the result.

items.s: Demand fell; ____, prices dropped.
items.note: 'Hence' means 'for this reason' in formal writing.

items.s: I like fruit, ____ apples and bananas.
items.note: 'Such as' introduces examples.

items.s: There are many options. ____, you could take the train.
items.note: 'For example' starts a new sentence.

items.s: Some tools, ____ Jira and Trello, help teams track tasks.
items.note: 'Such as' + examples inside a sentence.

items.s: Several departments, ____ HR and Finance, were affected.
items.note: 'Including' + noun phrase.

items.s: We need to cut costs; ____, by reducing travel.
items.note: 'For example' can introduce a phrase after a semicolon.

items.s: The contract has one major flaw, ____, the absence of a termination clause.
items.note: 'Namely' specifies exactly what you mean.

items.s: I'm particularly interested in security, ____ in access control.
items.note: 'Especially' highlights one item.

items.s: I do lots of sports, ____ running and swimming.
items.note: 'Like' = 'such as' informally.

items.s: ____, open the app. Then log in.
items.note: 'First' starts a sequence; 'then' follows.

items.s: I finished work, and ____ I went to the gym.
items.note: 'Then' shows the next action.

items.s: Let's order now. ____, we can talk.
items.note: 'Afterwards' = later.

items.s: The engineers are fixing the bug. ____, please use the backup server.
items.note: 'In the meantime' = while waiting.

items.s: We tried several fixes, and ____ the problem was resolved.
items.note: 'Eventually' = after a long effort.

items.s: The incident began at 09:12. ____, the team restored service at 10:05.
items.note: 'Subsequently' shows what came later in a formal report.

items.s: ____ of all, we need a clear budget.
items.note: 'First of all' is a fixed phrase.

items.s: Mix the flour and eggs. ____ add the milk slowly.
items.note: 'After that' shows the next step.

items.s: ____, the new design is not perfect, but it is a big improvement.
items.note: 'Admittedly' concedes a point.

items.s: ____ the traffic, we arrived on time.
items.note: 'Despite' + noun phrase.

items.s: ____ the traffic was heavy, we arrived on time.
items.note: 'Although' + full clause.

items.s: ____ his lack of experience, he handled the crisis well.
items.note: 'In spite of' + noun phrase.

items.s: ____, I think we should postpone the launch.
items.note: 'All things considered' gives a final judgement.

items.s: ____ my opinion, remote work is more productive.
items.note: The fixed phrase is 'In my opinion'.

items.s: To be ____ to him, he did warn us about the risks.
items.note: 'To be fair to him' adds balance.

items.s: It's not ideal; ____, it's the best we can afford.
items.note: 'Still' works as a concessive adverb meaning 'even so'.
